	## How the GPT should analyze audio (what Data Analysis can do)
	When you upload audio, it can run Python analysis (typical libraries: librosa; numpy; scipy). Practical metrics it can generate:
	- **Tempo estimate** (with confidence range)
	- **Spectral tilt** (is it dark; bright; harsh)
	- **Low-end integrity** (boom vs tight; bass/tom overlap)
	- **Stereo width + mono correlation**
	- **Dynamic range / crest factor** (is it crushed; too flat)
	- **Section change detection** (approximate: novelty curve)
	Then it maps those back to your prompt claims:
	- “tight pocket” vs actual transient smearing
	- “upright bass warm wood” vs sub-heavy mud
	- “lead front-and-center” vs vocal buried
	- “tape feel” vs sterile high-end

Then we pressure-test it until it becomes rock solid: auditable, peer-reviewable, BCDR-ready, zero-day-ready, cold-site-ready, red-team-ready. That has been my working method for thirty years.
	The dev sessions matter just as much as the product outputs because they contain the evolution of my understanding. Their value is not in the raw chat itself, but in the policies, procedures, processes, guardrails, and insights that become visible only in retrospect. Every exchange is provisional until the branch is complete. Earlier turns often do not reveal their real meaning until later turns force clarification, correction, or reinterpretation. That means the session is not actually “done” at any one turn. It is only complete at the end of the branch, when the full arc of the dialogue can be read as a whole. That full retrospective synthesis has never truly been performed, and without it, the product cannot be faithfully reformulated.
